strengths: The paper is well written and clearly structured, with a compelling motivating argument: classical SRs are policy-dependent and dominated by diffusion, so a temporally abstracted predictive representation (HSR) should be more robust for transfer in multi-compartmental environments.

The formal development is careful: the HSR Bellman operator (Eq. 5) is derived cleanly in Appendix A.1, and Theorem 3.1 (contraction under max-norm) is stated and proved, giving the online TD-learning rule (Eq. 8) a solid foundation.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: the paper tests three distinct hypotheses (transfer robustness, NMF vs. SVD decomposition, scalable exploration), uses appropriate baselines (one-hot, RW-SR, expected SR with the same pretraining distribution, SR-GPI), applies statistical tests with reported p-values, and uses 10-20 random seeds.

Key design choices are ablated rather than asserted: robustness across environments (Fig. S3), option classes including covering and random options (Fig. S4), number of options (Fig. S4d,e), and online vs. offline option construction (Fig. 2i-l, Fig. S6). The negative results for NMF on standard SRs and for SVD on HSRs support the 'feature collapse vs. piecewise-smooth topology' argument.

The comparison with SR-GPI (Section 4.3) is honest and shows HSR is complementary rather than strictly superior, and the discussion candidly acknowledges that experiments are restricted to discrete tabular settings and that the online option-construction procedure is heuristic.

The exploration results (Figure 6, S6) extend the contribution beyond transfer, showing that HSR-SPIE maintains asymptotic coverage as maze size grows where SR-SPIE degrades, with online option construction remaining viable.
weaknesses: The core construction has limited technical novelty: the HSR is essentially the successor representation of the semi-MDP induced by options, which follows directly from the options framework (Sutton et al., 1999) and the SMDP value decomposition. The paper does not precisely situate HSR relative to this prior formulation or to successor features over options, so the distinction between 'extension of SR' and 'standard SMDP SR' is underexplored. Theorem 3.1 is a routine contraction proof.

All experiments are in small, discrete, tabular grid-worlds (four-room and procedurally generated mazes). The claimed benefits (robust transfer, interpretable topological basis, scalable exploration) are most valuable in high-dimensional or continuous domains, where the paper offers no evidence; function approximation, which is central to modern practice, is only linear over tabular features.

The expected-HSR (eHSR) construction assumes access to a distribution of pre-training tasks with the same transition dynamics, which weakens the claim of robustness 'with respect to the existence of a pre-training phase' relative to GPI-based methods; the online option-construction procedure is admittedly heuristic and lacks theoretical analysis of its convergence or representation quality.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the implementation section states that code 'can be found at' but the repository link is blank in the manuscript, and some experimental details (e.g., how pre-training task distributions are sampled, NMF initialization and rank selection) are only lightly specified.

The theoretical analysis of when HSR-NMF should recover interpretable topological structure is informal; the argument leans on visual evidence (t-SNE, basis plots) and the Donoho-Stodden separability citation without formal conditions verified for the studied environments.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., 'policy-agnostic hierarchical map' and 'bridges model-free optimality and model-based flexibility' are supported only qualitatively; and the HSR-NMF advantage over SR baselines in Figure 3 partly depends on the choice of K=N=104 bases, whose sensitivity is not fully explored.

strengths: The core formalism is developed carefully: the HSR Bellman operator is derived from first principles (Appendix A.1), shown to be a contraction (Theorem 3.1), and an online TD-learning rule (Equation 8) follows naturally, mirroring the classical SR framework.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: 20 random seeds, formal statistical tests (two-sample t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank, two-way ANOVA), and multiple controls including an 'expected SR' baseline constructed from the identical pre-training task distribution (Figure 1a), which fairly isolates the contribution of temporal abstraction from that of averaging over tasks.

Robustness is probed systematically rather than cherry-picked: transfer results are replicated across four grid-world topologies (Figure S3), three option classes (Figure S4), varying option budgets (4–32, Figure S4e), online vs. offline option construction (Figures 2j–l, S6), and SR-GPI is included as a complementary algorithmic baseline (Section 4.3).

The mechanism is investigated, not just the headline numbers: representation drift is quantified (Figure 2g), value-function reconstruction R² is measured against dynamic programming ground truth (Figures 2h, 4d), basis activations along trajectories are visualised (Figure 4b), and the NMF-vs-SVD argument is grounded in the 'feature collapse' vs. 'piecewise-smooth' geometric analysis (Figures 1g, 1i–j).

The limitations section is candid: the authors explicitly acknowledge restriction to discrete tabular MDPs, the heuristic nature of the online option-construction procedure, and the confounds that deep function approximation would introduce.
weaknesses: Restricted empirical scope: all experiments are in tabular grid-worlds (four-room variants up to ~104 states, mazes up to 50×50). The central claims concern robust transfer and scalability under non-stationary policies; without any continuous-state or deep-RL evidence, the practical significance for the broader ICML audience remains unproven, and the authors themselves flag deep RL as future work.

Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially the successor representation of the option-augmented MDP (the SR of the SMDP induced by a high-level policy), combined with the well-established eigenoption construction (Machado et al., 2017) and NMF (Lee & Seung, 1999). Each ingredient is standard; the contraction result (Theorem 3.1) is a one-line corollary of τ ≥ 1 rather than a substantive theoretical contribution.

Internal tension regarding the pre-training requirement: the paper criticises GPI algorithms for 'critically hinging on the two-stage process involving pre-training' (Section 5), yet the strongest results (eHSR, HSR-NMF, Figures 3–4) require a pre-training task distribution to build the expected HSR, and the policy-robustness argument partly reduces to averaging over a set of optimal policies for the same transition dynamics.

Policy dependence is weakened, not eliminated: the HSR is still conditioned on the high-level policy μ over options; the claim of a 'policy-agnostic' representation holds only under fixed transition dynamics and a fixed option set, and the discussion of when HSR features would be invalidated (e.g., transition changes, non-stationary option sets) is deferred to future work.

Reproducibility gap: Appendix C states 'Python codes for empirical evaluations included in the main paper can be found at' with the URL missing/empty, which undermines the otherwise detailed implementation description.

Presentation and reporting issues that should be fixed: caption error in Figure 1 ('Same as j, but for the RW-SR matrix' should read i); a garbled p-value in Figure S6 ('p = 8.7071 × 1−−18'); inconsistent test descriptions (Figure 5c labels a 'two-sided two-sample paired t-test'); several typos ('An related class', 'confound', 'The same set of hyperparameters is used...'). Some statistical choices also warrant clarification (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank reported for what appear to be independent agent runs in Figure 3b).

The exploration analysis leaves an unexplained anomaly: HSR-norm intrinsic reward yields slower state coverage yet better goal discovery (Figure 6b), which is acknowledged as 'somewhat surprising' but only qualitatively rationalised.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: classical SRs are policy-dependent and dominated by spectral diffusion, and incorporating temporally extended options into the predictive representation is a principled way to address both limitations.

The technical framework is sound and carefully developed: the HSR Bellman operator (Equation 5), the discounted termination kernel (Equation 6), and the derivation of the TD update rule (Equation 8) are clean, with a full derivation in Appendix A and a correct contraction proof (Theorem 3.1).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this class of work: multiple grid-world topologies (Figure S3), ablations over option classes (eigenoptions vs. covering vs. random options) and option budgets (Figure S4), a fair eSR baseline isolating the effect of temporal abstraction from the effect of the options themselves, pre-trained vs. online-learned representations, and statistical tests with reported effect sizes.

The NMF-vs-SVD analysis is insightful: the argument that HSR's piecewise-smooth structure makes non-negative factorisation well-posed while SR features suffer 'feature collapse' is supported by visual (Figure 1h-j, Figure S1) and quantitative (Figure 4) evidence, including the whack-a-mole/bottleneck activation analysis.

The paper demonstrates utility beyond transfer, connecting to GPI (Section 4.3) and scalable intrinsically motivated exploration in procedurally generated mazes (Section 4.4), and shows the framework works with online-constructed options, mitigating the two-stage pretraining dependency.
Reproducibility is well handled: pseudocode for all algorithms (S1-S3), full hyperparameter specifications, and a public code repository.
The limitations are discussed honestly (tabular/discrete settings only, heuristic online option-construction procedure) rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is limited to small, discrete, tabular grid-worlds with linear function approximation. While the authors acknowledge this and argue for controlled confounds, the central claims of 'robust transfer' and 'scalable exploration' are only demonstrated at a scale (N ~ 10^2-10^4 states) where SRs are known to be well-behaved; whether HSR-NMF remains tractable or beneficial with function approximation in high-dimensional domains is unresolved.

The novelty is incremental in parts: the construction is essentially an SR over a semi-MDP induced by an option set, and related machinery (option-conditional predictions, hierarchical value function decompositions, successor features over temporally extended actions) exists in prior work. The paper does not deeply discuss why this specific combination is distinct from those formulations beyond the eigenoption instantiation.

Some headline results are 'comparable' rather than superior: in the GPI experiments (Figure 5c), HSR-GPI matches but does not clearly beat SR-GPI (p = 0.199 vs. one-hot baseline), and HSR-norm intrinsic rewards are explicitly reported to be slower than SR-based ones in sparse-reward navigation (Section 4.4), which qualifies the breadth of the advantages.

The claim that NMF uniquely enables HSR-based generalisation rests largely on empirical comparisons; the conditions under which NMF recovers meaningful structure (e.g., separability assumptions from Donoho & Stodden) are invoked informally and not verified for the HSR matrices at hand.

The online option-construction procedure is acknowledged to be heuristic and simple, with no theoretical guarantees; since several results rely on it, the framework's guarantees are therefore confined to the offline, pre-trained option setting.
NMF introduces additional hyperparameters (K, initialisation, multiple restarts) and computational cost relative to SVD whose practical sensitivity is not fully characterised.
